title: Low serum thyrotropin concentrations as a risk factor for atrial fibrillation in older persons
authors: Sawin CT, Geller A, Wolf PA, Belanger AJ, Baker E, Bacharach P, et al.
population: Framingham Heart Study participants aged 60 years or older without atrial fibrillation at the 15th biennial examination (1978 to 1980); 814 men and 1193 women
funder: Supported in part by the Medical Research Service, Department of Veterans Affairs; by grants from the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (2-R01-NS-17950-12), the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (R01-HL40423-04), and Boots Pharmaceuticals; and by a contract (NO1-HC-38038) with the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
result: Atrial fibrillation occurred in 13 of 61 people with TSH 0.1 mU/l or lower, 23 of 187 with 0.1 to 0.4, 133 of 1576 with 0.4 to 5.0 and 23 of 183 above 5.0. Cumulative 10-year incidence 28% with TSH 0.1 or lower against 11% with normal TSH; age-adjusted incidence 28 against 10 per 1000 person-years; adjusted relative risk 3.1 (95% CI 1.7 to 5.5). Thirty of the 46 people with low TSH who did not develop atrial fibrillation or overt hyperthyroidism were taking thyroid hormone; excluding subjects taking thyroid hormone had only a limited effect on the relative risks. The authors state that in people receiving thyroid hormone with low TSH the risk can be lessened by avoiding excessively high doses.
